extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: scientists, educators, and professional researchers (early 20th-century British scientific community)
extracted.subtask_description: This page contains book reviews (embryology, crystallography, physics textbooks) and academic/instrument advertisements and job listings; the implicit criteria are standards for evaluating scientific books, textbooks, laboratory apparatus, and applications for academic posts. Extracted rubrics cover what makes these books/instruments/appointments acceptable or desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful and graphic representation in a hand-atlas
rubrics_metrics.description: A hand-atlas should provide 'a truthful and graphic representation of our present knowledge concerning the conception and development of the human body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review praises an atlas that functions 'more like a museum than a book' by collecting specimens from the best sources and illustrating nearly all stages; it should contain numerous high-quality figures (the reviewed work contains ~800 figures) each with a brief explanatory text to serve the place of a catalogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reconstruction methods for embryological accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimens should be cut, fixed, sectionised, and accurately reconstructed (e.g., by wax-plate reconstruction) to permit faithful representation and easy mutual exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruction allows rapid demonstration of material that took months to acquire; the review notes the method's provenance and that many high-quality reconstructions were produced in Germany, Switzerland, and America, implying a standard for rigorous preparation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative embryology to fill observational gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct human observations are lacking (e.g., fertilisation and segmentation), a work should draw on comparative illustrations from other mammals to supply likely forms and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewed atlas reproduces mouse, dog, and bat illustrations to represent early stages; authors are commended for drawing freely on established comparative embryological work (Sobotta, Bonnet, van Beneden, van Wijhe, Flemming, Hertwig, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration and discussion of developmental abnormalities
rubrics_metrics.description: A comprehensive embryological work should include and illustrate abnormalities of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion of abnormal development is listed among the atlas's contents, implying completeness and usefulness for study of normal and pathological variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, lucid exposition covering core subtopics
rubrics_metrics.description: An introductory book (e.g., on crystallography) should be concise and lucid while covering main aspects such as polymorphism, morphotropy, isomorphism, and molecular compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review values briefness and clarity and notes the need to incorporate recent research developments (e.g., close-packing theory) in revisions, recommending such introductions to chemists unfamiliar with the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency with recent research
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific texts should incorporate recent investigations and be revised when significant new material appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The crystallography introduction included some alterations due to investigations published between original and translation, but further revision was still demanded by still more recent material (Barlow and Pope's close-packing theory is cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of practical physics course to target students
rubrics_metrics.description: A first-year practical physics course should be accessible to pupils in day schools, evening schools, and pupil-teacher classes—not too difficult yet containing all that is really essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer approves a course that limits theory in the text (leaving theory to the teacher in the first year) and focuses on essential experimental practice appropriate to novices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orderliness and clarity of experimental instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of experiments should be clear and presented in a logical order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The First Year's Course is commended because 'the instructions given seem to be very clear in the main, and the order of experiment is quite logical.' Clarity of steps and sequence is a mark of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential experimental content coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: A beginner practical course should include core measurements and simple experiments: length, area, volume, mass, relative density, air pressure, and some heat experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer lists these topics as constituting an appropriate and sufficient first-year experimental curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental pedagogy: providing experiments without prescriptive theory
rubrics_metrics.description: For beginners, experiment descriptions can omit extended theory so that the teacher provides explanatory context; students are guided in technique first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The First Year's Course deliberately presents experiments 'not surrounded by any theory,' with the opinion that the teacher should supply theory in the first year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook design for specific educational contexts (evening artisans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks intended for particular audiences (e.g., artisans in evening schools) should be tailored to their needs—principally practical and experimental instruction relevant to trades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mackenzie's volume is praised as 'intended for artisans' and 'wholly experimental,' addressing an underserved class; suitability to audience and practical relevance are key criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of guidance: detailed procedures but open-ended observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good experimental manuals may give detailed procedural instructions while not always telling students explicitly what they are expected to see or which conclusions to draw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mackenzie's book 'gives instructions on the carrying out of experiments in detail' yet often 'the students are not told ... what conclusions they should draw,' which the reviewer presents as a pedagogical choice (suitable introduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic appointment application requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications for teaching posts should show formal qualifications (university degree or equivalent), copies of testimonials, often residency terms (resident), and be submitted on prescribed forms by stated deadlines, sometimes accompanied by a stamped, addressed envelope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple listings specify 'University degree, or its equivalent,' 'copies of testimonials must reach the registrar not later than [date],' 'resident,' 'copies of form upon which application is to be made obtained by sending stamped, addressed, foolscap envelope,' and similar procedural details—these are mandatory administrative/eligibility criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory assistant appointment qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants for laboratory assistant posts should have training in a physical or chemical laboratory and strong mathematical qualifications; applications must state age and qualifications and include references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Physical Laboratory vacancy requires 'training in a Physical or ... Laboratory... also high mathematical qualifications,' salary listed, and instructs applicants to send age, qualifications, and two references in writing to the Director by a deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument selection: performance and standard tests (Kew Observatory test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meteorological and scientific instruments for observatories or professional use should be of best quality and able to 'pass the Kew Observatory test'; certificates may be provided if desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Peandar' set is described as 'best quality' and able to pass the Kew Observatory test; Kew certificates are offered for a small extra charge—thus passing recognized standard tests is presented as a selection criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument selection: portability, robustness, and suitability to use-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Optical and field instruments should combine appropriate optical qualities (large flat field, improved definition), portability, and specific features for intended users (naturalists, tourists, marine work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads for Platyscopic pocket lens, prism binoculars, and field glasses emphasize attributes: larger angles, increased field, improved definition, focusing distance, flat field for opaque objects, various powers, leather-mounted cases, and types specialized for tourists or naturalists—these product specs function as selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus performance metrics (liquefiers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laboratory apparatus (e.g., air-liquefiers) should have measurable performance traits: compactness, short liquefaction time (6–10 minutes), production rate (over 1 litre per hour), no auxiliary refrigerant needed, and operator simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hampson's air-liquefier advertises these concrete performance measures and user-friendliness (one gauge and one valve), implying these are expected standards when choosing such apparatus.
